p: A **two-way table** shows two kinds of information at once – for example gender and favourite sport. Each row and each column has a **total**.
In the table, 12 boys chose football, 17 boys were asked and 35 students were asked altogether.

lesson.t: How do I find missing values?
p: Every row adds up to its row total and every column adds up to its column total.
The **grand total** (bottom right) equals the sum of the row totals **and** the sum of the column totals: row totals 12 and 18 → grand total 30.

lesson.t: How do I complete a two-way table?
p: Step 1: Find a row or column with only one missing value.
Step 2: Add or subtract to find it.
Step 3: Repeat until the table is full.
Step 4: Check: rows and columns both add to the grand total.

lesson.t: What are dual and compound bar charts?
p: A **dual bar chart** puts bars for two groups **side by side** for each category, so you can compare the groups. In the chart, the boys (B) and girls (G) for each day stand next to each other.
A **compound (stacked) bar chart** stacks the groups in **one bar** per category. The height of the whole bar shows the **total**; the sections show the parts.
Use a **dual** bar chart to compare the groups within each category (boys vs girls each day).
Use a **compound** bar chart to compare **totals** (which day had most students) while still seeing the parts.

lesson.t: How do I draw a dual bar chart?
p: Step 1: Draw axes with a scale for frequency.
Step 2: For each category draw two bars next to each other, one per group, in two colours.
Step 3: Leave a gap between categories.
Step 4: Add a key and a title.

lesson.t: What does a pie chart show?
p: A **pie chart** shows how a whole is split into parts. Each **sector** is a fraction of the whole circle, so a fraction of the data.
In the pie chart above, Walk is half (50%), Bus a quarter (25%), Car 15% and Bike 10%.
The whole circle is **360°**. Each item gets **360° ÷ total**.
If 30 people were asked, each person is 360 ÷ 30 = **12°**; 7 people → 84°.
To read a pie chart: (angle ÷ 360) × total.
A **waffle diagram** is a 10 × 10 grid of 100 squares: each square is **1%**. 37 shaded squares = **37%**.

lesson.t: How do I draw a pie chart?
p: Step 1: Find the total frequency.
Step 2: Work out 360° ÷ total (degrees per item).
Step 3: Multiply each frequency by this to get its angle; check the angles add to 360°.
Step 4: Draw the sectors with a protractor and label them.

p: A bigger sector in a pie chart of 40 people may be fewer people than a smaller sector in a chart of 400. Pie charts show proportions.

p: An **infographic** presents data using pictures, icons, short text and simple charts, so information is quick to understand.
They are common in newspapers, websites and adverts.

lesson.t: What should I check on an infographic?
p: **Read the numbers**, not just the pictures: icons are sometimes drawn bigger or smaller than the data says, which can mislead.
Check the **source**, the **date** and **sample size** (how many people were asked), and whether percentages are of the same total.
Ask: what is the infographic trying to make me think? Is anything left out?

lesson.t: How do I comment on an infographic?
p: Step 1: State one fact it shows correctly.
Step 2: Check the pictures match the numbers.
Step 3: Comment on missing information (sample size, source) or misleading design.

lesson.q: An infographic shows 20% as a big icon and 40% as a smaller icon. What is wrong?
steps: The bigger icon shows the smaller value
lesson.a: The picture sizes do not match the numbers – it is misleading

lesson.q: '9 out of 10 owners prefer Brand X.' What would you want to know?
steps: How many owners were asked? Who asked them?
lesson.a: The sample size and who carried out the survey

p: Always read the actual values. Pictures are designed to catch attention, not to be accurate.
Name the exact feature that is misleading (scale, icon size, missing total).

lesson.t: How do I choose the right chart?

head: Data
Good choice
rows: pie chart, compound bar chart, waffle

p: A good chart makes the important pattern obvious. A **line graph** shows how a puppy's mass **changes over 6 months**; a pie chart could not show this.

Step 2: Ask: what do I want to show (comparison, proportion, change, relationship)?
Step 3: Choose the chart from the table and explain why.

lesson.t: What are the averages and the range?
p: **Mode**: the most common value. **Median**: the middle value when the data is in order. **Mean**: total ÷ number of values. **Range**: largest − smallest (spread, not an average).
For 3, 5, 9, 11: mean = 28 ÷ 4 = 7, median = (5 + 9) ÷ 2 = 7, range = 8, no mode.
**Mode**: for categorical data ('favourite colour') or the most popular size.
**Median**: when there are extreme values (outliers), because it is not pulled by them.
**Mean**: when you want to use all the data and there are no outliers.
Salaries 20, 22, 25, 26, 200 (thousand): the mean 58.6 is misleading; the median 25 is typical.

lesson.t: How do I compare two sets of data?
p: Compare an **average** (which is higher on average) and the **range** (which is more consistent), and write both **in context**.

lesson.t: How do I calculate all four?
p: Step 1: Order the data and count the values (n).
Step 2: Mode: most frequent. Median: value in position (n + 1) ÷ 2.
Step 3: Mean: total ÷ n.
Step 4: Range: largest − smallest.

lesson.q: Class A test marks: mean 62, range 15. Class B: mean 58, range 40. Compare.
lesson.a: Class A did better on average and its marks were more consistent.

p: The range measures **spread**. It says nothing about the typical value.
Compare one average and the range, each in a sentence about the real situation.
